title: JSON and CSV
description: Serializing and deserializing JSON data, and reading/writing CSV files, using the standard library.
objectives: Understand JSON structure and how it maps to Python types
Read and write CSV files with the csv module

content.heading: JSON: Serialization and Deserialization
content.body:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text-based data format built from objects ({...}, like a Python dict), arrays ([...], like a Python list), strings, numbers, booleans (true/false), and null — it maps very naturally onto Python's own built-in types. Serialization is converting a Python object into JSON text; deserialization is the reverse. json.dumps(obj) returns a JSON-formatted string from a Python object (dict/list/str/int/float/bool/None); json.loads(text) parses a JSON string back into the corresponding Python object. The file-oriented equivalents, json.dump(obj, file) and json.load(file), write to and read directly from an already-open file object, saving you the intermediate string step.

Not every Python object is JSON-serializable by default — only the types listed above and combinations of them; custom class instances need a conversion step (a default= function, or converting to a dict first) before they can be serialized.

content.heading: CSV: Reading and Writing
content.body: CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is a simple tabular text format, one row per line, fields separated by commas (or another delimiter). Hand-splitting lines on commas breaks down as soon as a field itself contains a comma or a quoted newline, so the csv module is the correct tool: csv.reader(file) iterates over a file yielding each row as a list of strings; csv.writer(file).writerow(row) (or writerows(rows) for many at once) writes a list of values as a properly comma-separated, quoted-when-necessary line. csv.DictReader and csv.DictWriter work the same way but read/write each row as a dict, using the first row as field names — often more convenient than tracking column positions by index.

content.code:
import json, csv

data = {"name": "Asha", "skills": ["Python", "SQL"]}
text = json.dumps(data)
print(text)                         # {"name": "Asha", "skills": ["Python", "SQL"]}
print(json.loads(text)["name"])     # Asha

with open("scores.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["name", "score"])
    writer.writerow(["Asha", 88])

with open("scores.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.reader(f):
        print(row)
content.explanation: json.dumps/loads round-trip a dict through JSON text. The csv writer/reader correctly handle the comma-separated format, including the header row, without manual string splitting.

keyPoints: JSON objects/arrays map to Python dicts/lists; only JSON-compatible types serialize directly
json.dumps()/loads() work with strings; json.dump()/load() work directly with file objects
Always use the csv module rather than hand-splitting on commas — it handles quoting correctly
csv.DictReader/DictWriter work with rows as dicts, keyed by the header row
commonMistakes: Hand-splitting CSV lines on "," and breaking on fields that contain commas or quotes
Trying to json.dumps() a custom object directly without first converting it to a dict
Forgetting newline="" when opening a CSV file for writing on some platforms, causing extra blank lines
